title: Documentation that survives: README, architecture notes, decision records

claims.text: Michael Nygard published Documenting Architecture Decisions on 15 November 2011. He describes a decision record as a short text file in a format similar to an Alexandrian pattern, where each record describes a set of forces and a single decision in response to those forces.

source.title: Nygard, M., Documenting Architecture Decisions, 15 November 2011

claims.text: Nygard argues that agile methods are not opposed to documentation, only to valueless documentation.

source.title: Nygard, M., Documenting Architecture Decisions, 15 November 2011

claims.text: The record format he gives contains a title, the context of the decision, the decision itself, and its consequences. Records are not deleted when a decision changes; a later record supersedes an earlier one.

source.title: Nygard, M., Documenting Architecture Decisions, 15 November 2011

claims.text: The approach builds on Kruchten’s work on the decision view’s role in software architecture practice, which extended an earlier view model to capture the rationale behind important decisions.

source.title: Nygard, M., Documenting Architecture Decisions, 15 November 2011

beats.broke: documentation describes the current state of a system, the system changes, and nothing in the mechanism makes the description change with it
beats.fix: write down things that cannot become false — a decision made at a time, with its context and consequences — and supersede rather than edit
beats.cost: a pile of decision records tells you the history and not the present, so it does not replace the document that rots
beats.interview: why a decision record does not go stale when a README does
